hero.headline: Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties could lose millions under property tax referendum
hero.teaser: A recent study from the Florida Association of Counties estimates Martin County could lose $50 million in 2027-28 and $93 million in 2028-29 under the new property tax reform referendum.
hero.body:
Government officials are working to assess the impact of the new property tax reform referendum that would raise the homestead exemption and lower property tax bills. A recent study from the Florida Association of Counties offered up estimates of the potential losses: Martin County faces $50 million in 2027-28 and $93 million in 2028-29, St. Lucie County faces $80 million in 2027-28 and $140 million in 2028-29, and Indian River County faces $32 million in 2027-28 and $57 million in 2028-29.

Palm Beach County Commissioner Bobby Powell said if there is a cut when it comes to property taxes, there will be some real shortfalls, some real challenges and some revenue will have to be made up somewhere. Powell said options like finding new revenue and budget cuts are a possibility, but officials do not yet know if it will be an increase in sales tax or an increase in user fees for other services.

State Rep. Toby Overdorf, R-Stuart, said the proposal is more of a break for the struggling family that is in a $300,000 home and working several jobs to make sure ends meet. The referendum to raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 will be decided by voters in November.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce pastor charged with child neglect after children found in deplorable conditions
cards.teaser: A Fort Pierce pastor faces child neglect charges after authorities discovered children in her care living in deplorable conditions.
cards.body:
A Fort Pierce pastor faces child neglect charges after authorities discovered children in her care living in deplorable conditions. The charges were filed Saturday following an investigation into the living situation.

The pastor was taken into custody after officials determined the conditions posed a danger to the children's welfare. Authorities have not released the number of children involved or their current placement.

The investigation revealed living conditions that failed to meet basic standards of care and safety. Law enforcement and child welfare agencies worked together on the case.

The pastor now faces multiple counts of child neglect. The case remains under investigation as authorities work to ensure the safety of all children who were under her supervision.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds speaks out after receiving death threats in Florida gubernatorial race
cards.teaser: Gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds faced two separate death threats while campaigning for the Republican nomination in the August primary.
cards.body:
Gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds is speaking out about threats on his life as he runs for the Republican nomination in the August primary. The Naples Republican in his third term in Congress faced one threat on social media last month after re-sharing President Donald Trump's endorsement in the Governor's race. A second person called Donalds' district office making similar threats, saying he was going to blow up the entire office. "Somebody just flat out said they were going to kill me," Donalds told radio host Mark Levin on Friday.

Donalds cited the assassination of conservative Charlie Kirk last year as an example of what happens when political opponents are demonized rather than treated as human beings. He considers himself a free speech absolutist but stressed the importance of being mindful of rhetoric to avoid creating an environment where someone takes it as their responsibility to harm another person. "That's just reprehensible to me," he said. Donalds noted that recent experience shows examples of viewpoints being used to justify political violence and that people have strong opinions but ultimately just want to go home and see their families. He said the incident strengthened his resolve to work hard to become the state's next governor and keep Florida the preeminent conservative and common sense state in America. Donalds is undeterred by the threats and expressing confidence in his position in the race to succeed Ron DeSantis.

cards.headline: Florida man arrested after chasing children on bikes with baseball bat
cards.teaser: A Florida man was arrested Saturday after allegedly chasing children riding bikes while wielding a baseball bat.
cards.body:
Authorities arrested a man who allegedly pursued children on bicycles while armed with a baseball bat. The incident occurred Saturday and prompted multiple calls to law enforcement.

Witnesses reported seeing the man chasing the children in a threatening manner with the bat. Police responded to the scene and located the suspect.

The man was taken into custody on charges related to the incident. No injuries to the children were reported in connection with the chase.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds calls for GOP unity as primary opponents demand debates
cards.teaser: Gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds says the Republican party should coalesce behind him, citing his 40-plus point polling lead and Trump's endorsement. Primary opponents Jay Collins and Paul Renner are demanding debates.
cards.body:
Byron Donalds declared himself the front-runner in the Republican gubernatorial race Friday and urged the party to unite behind his candidacy more than two months before the August 18 primary election. The Naples congressman made his appeal for party cohesion hours after Democrat Jerry Demings withdrew from the gubernatorial contest due to a prostate cancer diagnosis. With Demings out of the Democratic primary, Donalds argued that the general election effectively begins now, making it imperative for Republicans to consolidate support rather than engage in divisive primary battles.

Donalds pointed to several factors as evidence of his strength and viability. He cited his complete and total endorsement from President Donald Trump and highlighted polling data showing him leading by more than 40 points in multiple public surveys. The congressman has raised $81 million for his campaign so far and indicated he would prefer to preserve those resources for the general election rather than spend them fighting rival Republicans in the primary. He stressed that all other candidates currently poll in single digits and contended that continued infighting among Republicans only benefits Democrats. "At this point, fighting amongst Republicans only helps the Democrats end the Florida Dream we all love and cherish," Donalds said. He pledged to communicate directly with voters through town halls, community meetings, business roundtables, and door-knocking efforts rather than through debate stage appearances.

However, two of Donalds' main competitors reject his call for unity and are demanding that he participate in debates. Jay Collins launched The Collins Callout website Friday, framing the challenge in confrontational terms. "The callout is on the table, the only question left is whether Byron answers the bell, or keeps running," the site stated. Former House Speaker Paul Renner went further, releasing a video on social media claiming that neither Donalds nor Collins is willing to debate him. "Floridians deserve to see the differences between the candidates. Stop ducking and let's get on stage," Renner said.

The candidates' fundraising totals through the end of March reveal significant gaps in their resources. Donalds has far outraised his opponents, while Renner had accumulated more than $6 million and Collins approximately $1.75 million. Updated fundraising reports covering activity through May will be due June 10, providing fresh indicators of financial momentum heading into the final stretch of the primary campaign. These figures underscore Donalds' substantial advantage in the field as the race enters its final phase.

cards.headline: Dolphin Entanglements in Indian River Lagoon Rising, Scientists Say
cards.teaser: Wildlife scientists report a skyrocketing number of dolphins entangled in fishing line in the Indian River Lagoon.
cards.body:
Wildlife scientists expressed concern about the increasing number of dolphin and fishing line entanglement cases in the Indian River Lagoon. The incidents involve dolphins becoming trapped in fishing gear and other marine debris.

The rise in entanglement cases has alarmed researchers monitoring the lagoon's marine mammal population. Scientists tracking the issue say the number of dolphins affected by fishing line has increased significantly in recent months.

cards.headline: Jupiter Island commissioner warns town 'reapplying Band-Aid' as erosion threatens to split island
cards.teaser: A state report found Jupiter Island's entire 11.5-mile shoreline is critically eroded, with erosion so severe the ocean could break through at Peck Lake and split the island in half.
cards.body:
The 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report warned erosion threatens roads, buildings, drainage systems, natural habitats, wildlife and ancient sites on Jupiter Island. The threat stretches from Blowing Rocks Preserve to Peck Lake, where a breach could turn a thin strip of land into an open inlet. A storm breached Peck Lake in the early 1960s before the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers filled it back in with sand.

Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said the town continues to fight erosion through constant maintenance. In April 2025, the town completed a major beach renourishment project, dumping enough sand to fill nearly 400 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Field said about $3 million in town taxpayer dollars goes toward beach renourishment every year. He said no oceanfront homes are in immediate danger but only because of ongoing work.

Mark Perry with the Florida Oceanographic Society said the consequences extend well beyond the shoreline. The Joseph Reed Mound, a 3,000- to 4,000-year-old archaeological site, is already half lost to erosion, according to the report. Wildlife refuges including Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park are also at risk. Perry said over 33 threatened and endangered species inhabit those areas.

cards.headline: Florida voters divided on property tax proposal ahead of November ballot
cards.teaser: A ballot measure that would raise the homestead exemption to roll back property taxes needs 60% approval to pass in November. Cities and counties are still calculating how much money they would lose if the measure passes.
cards.body:
Florida voters will decide this November whether to raise the homestead exemption to roll back property taxes, a proposal drawing mixed reactions from West Palm Beach residents. The ballot measure requires 60% approval to pass. A similar proposal failed in 2018.

Rosabella Olivares, a shopper in West Palm Beach, expressed concern about reduced funding. "There's going to be less money because everything is expensive now," she said. Brian Edington supports the idea because it benefits homeowners who permanently live in Florida. He said he is comfortable with local governments spending less and pointed to trash services in his neighborhood as an example, noting that twice-weekly pickup is unnecessary when once weekly would be adequate. A resident identified as Stan said he does not want funding eliminated entirely, saying "infrastructure and all that stuff is important, but if they can lower it to help the people out some." Another resident said the system should be tied more directly to services people actually use, explaining he would not mind paying more while his child is in school but should not have to pay for school services when the child is out of school. However, renters expressed skepticism that savings would reach them. One resident on Clematis Avenue in downtown West Palm Beach said landlords will raise rent on all renters.

cards.headline: State weighs statewide fireworks ban for Fourth of July due to severe drought
cards.teaser: Florida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson warned the state may ban fireworks for the Fourth of July's 250th anniversary celebration if drought conditions persist.
cards.body:
The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services is evaluating a statewide fireworks ban for Fourth of July celebrations due to severe drought conditions. The current drought is more severe than 1998, the last time Florida implemented such a ban. The entire state is at least abnormally dry, with Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast experiencing moderate to extreme drought conditions.

Florida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson issued an early warning in May about the possibility of a ban. Simpson stated that if drought conditions persist through Fourth of July, a ban is likely. He warned that hundreds of thousands of people using fireworks could put the entire state on fire in one evening. Simpson acknowledged the significance of this year's 250th anniversary celebration but urged residents to consider alternatives. Meanwhile, Bill Murphy of Sky King Fireworks in West Palm Beach said the store has seen increased customer activity ahead of the holiday. Murphy said the store monitors drought conditions closely but remains cautiously optimistic, noting that rain is forecasted. The Department of Agriculture indicated that a fireworks ban would be a last resort.

cards.headline: Rental assistance applications fill within hours as demand outweighs funding in Palm Beach County
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County receives nearly 8,000 calls for housing assistance per month and typically receives about 600 applications in the first couple hours after opening.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County's Community Services Department has nearly $2 million in combined grant funding for its Emergency Rental Assistance Program. Applications open at the beginning of each month but fill quickly, with the county typically receiving about 600 applications in the first couple of hours. Dr. James Green, program director, said the county currently has about 800 applications in the queue for rental assistance and receives nearly 8,000 calls for housing assistance per month combined with 211. At the time of the report, the county's assistance portal was marked closed due to high demand. Green urges anyone in need to call 1-833-CSD-WILL to check for availability.

According to the Department of Housing and Urban Development, the average rent for a one-bedroom in Palm Beach County is $2,020 a month. Joanne Bromfield, who recently moved to West Palm Beach from Tampa, said she had to switch her career just to afford rent. Bromfield, who spent 12 years as an educator, switched to real estate hoping for a higher income. She said she worries about paying rent almost every day because all the bills are rising except paychecks. Green said the recent surge in applications is partly due to rising costs of living including housing, gas and food. For those who cannot get into the county's program, 211 is another option that connects callers with nonprofits and other assistance programs 24/7. Green is calling on people with extra housing to partner with the county to help neighbors in need.

cards.headline: Florida shark dive operators fight federal feeding ban threatening Treasure Coast businesses
cards.teaser: A federal proposal to ban shark feeding off Florida's coast within 200 miles cleared the U.S. House and drew sharp criticism from dive operators who warn it could devastate conservation-driven tourism businesses.
cards.body:
H.R. 3831, known as the Safe Florida Seas Act, would prohibit shark feeding in federal waters within 200 miles of Florida, with an exception for harvesting. Nathan Campbell, owner of Emerald Charters, said Congress has not asked operators to present data or explain their practices. Campbell said the industry is requesting the chance to speak and share the science and facts before regulators eliminate shark diving operations.

Operators say they avoid surface chumming, instead taking bait underwater during dives. They argue this is less likely to condition sharks to approach boats looking for food, unlike some commercial harvesting operations that can release hundreds of gallons of chum at the surface. Dr. Matt Ajemian, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University, says shark diving in Florida has a near perfect safety record for customers. Campbell said that since Hawaii's 2006 ban on baited shark diving in federal waters, shark incidents have increased and fatalities have been reported. According to the Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council, at least one in four fishing trips in Hawaii ends with a shark biting off part of the catch.

cards.headline: 35 foster youth graduate at ChildNet celebration in Palm Beach County
cards.teaser: ChildNet held its annual graduation celebration at Palm Beach State College on Saturday, honoring 35 students served by the Broward and Palm Beach County nonprofit.
cards.body:
Thirty-five foster youth and young adults graduated at ChildNet's annual celebration held at Palm Beach State College, marking a significant milestone for the Broward and Palm Beach County nonprofit. Among the graduates were Sabrina Diaz and Brian Saintfort, both of whom lost a parent and turned to ChildNet for support. The organization equipped them with the resources needed to move forward. Diaz is already enrolled in pre-med classes at Palm Beach State College, where she hopes to become a doctor. Saintfort plans to pursue a vocational program to become a plumber.

The graduates shared messages of perseverance with others facing similar circumstances. Diaz urged them to believe they will be big one day, put effort into it, never give up on school, and never give up on dreams. Saintfort echoed the sentiment, saying to believe you will make it, then you're going to make it. Larry N. Rein, CEO of ChildNet, reflected on the evening's significance, calling it the fruition of great work by everyone in the community, including case workers at ChildNet and DCF, and especially the kids who worked so hard. ChildNet supports foster kids and young men and women through education, adoptions and independent living resources.

cards.headline: Fertilizer ban takes effect in Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties
cards.body:
Starting June 30, residents in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties must stop using fertilizers containing phosphorus or nitrogen on their lawns and landscaping. The ban applies during Florida's rainy season to reduce nutrient-rich runoff that flows into local waterways. According to Jordan Skaggs, with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, this runoff causes algae blooms that can disrupt the Indian River Lagoon and St. Lucie River. "It can shade out beneficial plants to fish and wildlife," Skaggs said. At certain densities, harmful algae blooms can release toxins that affect human health, wildlife health and overall ecosystem health.

Grantly Ricketts, director of University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommends composting as an alternative during the ban period. "It can be like a small trash can," Ricketts said. "That is the easiest and most practical way or means to add nutrients to your landscape." This method allows residents to add nutrients to their gardens and landscaping without using commercial fertilizers.

hero.headline: Masked intruder arrested after Port St. Lucie apartment break-in, $300 watch stolen
hero.teaser: A masked intruder broke into a Port St. Lucie apartment and stole a $300 watch before being arrested by police.
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie police arrested a suspect who broke into an apartment while wearing a mask. The intruder took a watch valued at $300 during the burglary.

Video evidence captured the masked suspect during the break-in. Police used the footage as part of their investigation leading to the arrest.

The suspect was taken into custody and charged in connection with the apartment burglary. The investigation included video documentation of the crime.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie homeowner's security camera leads to burglary arrest
cards.teaser: A Port St. Lucie man was arrested Saturday after a homeowner spotted a burglary in progress on a security camera.
cards.body:
A Port St. Lucie resident watching a home security camera system remotely observed a burglary taking place and alerted police. Officers responded to the call and arrested the suspect at the scene.

The homeowner's real-time monitoring of the security footage allowed for immediate notification of law enforcement. Police arrived while the burglary was still in progress.

The Port St. Lucie man was taken into custody and faces burglary charges. The case demonstrates the effectiveness of home security systems in helping solve crimes.

cards.headline: Self-described sovereign citizen arrested at Florida Walmart following disturbance
cards.teaser: A person identifying as a sovereign citizen was arrested at a Florida Walmart after causing a disturbance at the store.
cards.body:
Police arrested an individual at a Walmart location in Florida after the person caused a disturbance and identified as a sovereign citizen. The incident occurred Saturday and required law enforcement intervention.

Sovereign citizens typically reject government authority and claim immunity from laws. The individual's claims did not prevent arrest when the disturbance escalated.

Officers took the person into custody at the Walmart. The arrest followed standard procedures despite the suspect's assertions of sovereign status.

cards.headline: Okeechobee County woman sues Campbell Soup and Walmart over parasites in SpaghettiOs
cards.teaser: Mary Hubbard of Okeechobee County says she and her daughter found live worms in SpaghettiOs purchased at the Walmart Supercenter on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee in June 2024.
cards.body:
Mary Hubbard of Okeechobee County claims she and her daughter found live worms in their SpaghettiOs after eating them and is now suing Campbell Soup Co. and Walmart. According to the complaint, Hubbard purchased the SpaghettiOs at the Walmart Supercenter on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee in June 2024. Hubbard alleges she and her daughter developed parasitic infections and other medical complications as a result.

Attorneys for Hubbard stated she discovered what appeared to be worms or parasites actively moving within the food. The complaint notes that Hubbard documented the contamination in multiple videos, which clearly depict worm-like organisms moving within the food product. The lawsuit alleges the companies failed to properly inspect the product and seeks $50,000 in damages. Campbell Soup Co. said the claims lack merit, and Walmart said it is reviewing the court filing.

cards.headline: Florida Agriculture Commissioner warns Fourth of July fireworks ban possible due to drought
cards.teaser: Florida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson issued an early warning that fireworks could be banned for the Fourth of July if drought conditions persist.
cards.body:
Florida's Fourth of July celebrations could look significantly different this year as state leaders weigh whether to ban fireworks due to severe drought conditions. The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services says this year's drought is even more severe than 1998, the last time a statewide fireworks ban was put in place. The entire state of Florida is at least abnormally dry, with Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast experiencing moderate to extreme drought conditions.

Florida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson issued an early warning about a possible ban, stating that hundreds of thousands of people using fireworks simultaneously could put the entire state on fire in the evening. Simpson acknowledged the significance of this year's 250th anniversary celebration but urged residents to consider alternatives. At Sky King Fireworks in West Palm Beach, owner Bill Murphy reported increased customer activity ahead of the holiday. cards.headline: Florida shark dive operators fight federal shark feeding ban off state coast
cards.teaser: A federal proposal to ban shark feeding off Florida's coast is drawing sharp criticism from dive operators, including Nathan Campbell of Emerald Charters.
cards.body:
A federal proposal to ban shark feeding off Florida's coast is drawing sharp criticism from the state's shark diving industry, with operators warning it could devastate conservation-driven tourism businesses. The measure, H.R. 3831, known as the Safe Florida Seas Act, cleared the U.S. House and would prohibit shark feeding in federal waters within 200 miles of Florida, with an exception for harvesting. A coalition of dive operators says the bill unfairly targets their work, often veteran-owned small businesses and nonprofits focused on education and conservation, while leaving fishing practices untouched.

Nathan Campbell, owner of Emerald Charters, said operators are requesting the chance to speak and share the science and facts. "No one from Congress has yet asked us to present data or explain our practices," Campbell said. Operators say they avoid surface chumming, instead taking bait underwater during dives, arguing this is less likely to condition sharks to approach boats looking for food, unlike some commercial harvesting operations that can release hundreds of gallons of chum at the surface. Dr. Matt Ajemian, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University, says shark diving in Florida has a "near perfect safety record" for customers. In a letter to Congress, Campbell urged senators to delay action, gather research and involve all stakeholders in shaping any new rules.

cards.headline: Indian River Mall demolition underway in Vero Beach for mixed-use redevelopment
cards.body:
Demolition of the Indian River Mall began this week in Vero Beach as part of a revitalization project. Joseph Scarfone, the project manager, said crews are currently working on the first phase, which involves taking down the Macy's building and the former Sears location. Scarfone said the site will be transformed into a new indoor and outdoor shopping center spanning approximately 300,000 square feet, featuring retail, restaurants, and possible residential spaces.

Neighbors gathered in the mall parking lot to watch the demolition. Mary Alice Stopyra, a nearby resident, said she was happy about the project, noting the mall "degraded over time." Mark Manera, a Vero Beach resident who visited the mall regularly, described it as "a graveyard" with "a steady decline year after year after year." He said change is needed, adding that if the redevelopment brings "new life, new jobs, new opportunity, that's wonderful." Scarfone said the first phase is targeted for completion by 2027, and the team is still working on permitting for the remaining phases of the project.

hero.headline: St. Lucie, Martin, Indian River counties face millions in potential tax revenue losses under property tax referendum
hero.body:
Three Treasure Coast counties could see significant drops in property tax revenue if voters approve a November referendum to expand the homestead exemption, according to research from the Florida Association of Counties.

St. Lucie County estimates it could lose $80 million in 2027-28 and $140 million in 2028-29. Martin County projects losses of $50 million in 2027-28 and $93 million in 2028-29. Indian River County expects to lose $32 million in 2027-28 and $57 million in 2028-29. The referendum would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, which would lower property tax bills for eligible homeowners. The savings could range from hundreds to thousands of dollars depending on the county, city, and assessed home value.

Local government officials are now assessing how these revenue losses could affect services and budgets. Palm Beach County Commissioner Bobby Powell said officials are working with their administrator and the Office of Management and Budget to understand the impact. Powell acknowledged that if property taxes are cut, local governments will face real shortfalls and challenges, requiring new revenue sources or budget cuts. He suggested potential solutions could include increases in sales tax or user fees for other services, though he emphasized no decisions have been made. "We don't know if it will be an increase in sales tax, we don't know if it will be an increase in user fees for other services, we don't know right now," Powell said. While local officials are restricted by state law from opposing or endorsing the referendum, they can provide educational information to the public.

Republican lawmakers, including Governor Ron DeSantis, argue that local governments collect too much tax revenue and spend excessively. State Representative Toby Overdorf, R-Stuart, characterized the proposal as providing relief to working families struggling to afford homes. "This is more of a break for the struggling family that is in a $300,000 home and working several jobs to make sure ends meet," Overdorf said. He expressed support for allowing voters to decide the issue.

The referendum requires 60 percent approval to pass. A similar homestead exemption proposal failed in 2018. In Palm Beach County, over half of properties currently have the homestead exemption, which is higher than the state average of 47 percent. The November vote will determine whether the expanded exemption becomes law.

hero.headline: 80-Mile Ocean Paddle from Bimini to Lake Worth Beach Set for June 13
hero.teaser: More than 100 paddlers will launch from Bimini, Bahamas, at midnight on June 13, crossing 80 miles of open Atlantic Ocean to reach Lake Worth Beach after 12 to 16 hours of paddling to raise funds for cystic fibrosis families.
hero.body:
The annual Crossing for Cystic Fibrosis will bring more than 100 paddlers to Lake Worth Beach on June 13 after an 80-mile endurance trek from Bimini, Bahamas. According to event founder Travis Suit, participants will launch at midnight and arrive after 12 to 16 hours of paddling. The event benefits the Pipers Angels Foundation, which Suit established in honor of his daughter, Piper, diagnosed with cystic fibrosis at age 4.

The crossing is part of a four-day schedule beginning June 10 with arrivals and a poolside social at Bimini Cove. On Thursday, participants take part in a 4Ocean beach cleanup and a community buffet dinner. Friday brings a Paddle Out Rose Ceremony to honor cystic fibrosis warriors, followed by rest and safety checks before launch night.

All paddlers are required to wear a U.S. Coast Guard-approved personal flotation device, waterproof whistle, and reflective gear during dark hours. GPS trackers provided by the event must be worn and active at all times, and mandatory safety meetings will be held. Paddlers must raise at least $2,000 for the cause, with final contributions due July 31. Spectators are invited to Lake Worth Beach on June 13 to cheer paddlers during a daylong beach celebration marking their arrival. More information is available at crossingforcysticfibrosis.com and pipersangels.org.

cards.headline: Beetlejuice the Musical Closes Sunday at West Palm Beach's Kravis Center
cards.body:
"Beetlejuice" the musical brings spooky humor and over-the-top visuals to the Kravis Center in West Palm Beach, running June 2 through June 7 at the Alexander W. Dreyfoos Concert Hall. Actor Ryan Stajmiger plays the mischievous demon from Tim Burton's 1988 film. "I've loved the movie since I was a kid. I'm a huge Tim Burton fan, and you know, Michael Keaton's performance is so iconic," Stajmiger told WPTV. Though Keaton appears for only 15 minutes in the original film, his portrayal has lasted in audiences' memories. The musical follows Lydia Deetz, a "strange and unusual" teen whose life changes after meeting two recently deceased neighbors and a demon with a flair for trouble.

One of Stajmiger's favorite aspects of performing is breaking the fourth wall to communicate directly with the audience. Early in the run, he experienced an unexpected moment when his wig change went unplanned. During a scene where he wore two wigs, the second wig came off along with the first, leaving him bald for the entire scene. "I got to play with that a little bit, and got to experience everyone seeing me for the first time and not knowing that I am bald," he recalled. Performances are scheduled for 7:30 p.m. on June 3 and 4, 8 p.m. on June 5, matinee and evening shows on June 6, and a closing matinee on June 7. Tickets start at $34.50 at kravis.org. The show is recommended for ages 13 and up, with parental discretion advised.

hero.headline: Byron Donalds calls for GOP unity as primary opponents demand debates
hero.teaser: Gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds says the Republican party should coalesce behind him, citing his 40-plus point polling lead and Trump's endorsement. Primary opponents Jay Collins and Paul Renner are demanding debates.
hero.body:
Byron Donalds declared himself the front-runner in the Republican gubernatorial race Friday and urged the party to unite behind his candidacy more than two months before the August 18 primary election. The Naples congressman made his appeal for party cohesion hours after Democrat Jerry Demings withdrew from the gubernatorial contest due to a prostate cancer diagnosis. With Demings out of the Democratic primary, Donalds argued that the general election effectively begins now, making it imperative for Republicans to consolidate support rather than engage in divisive primary battles.

Donalds pointed to several factors as evidence of his strength and viability. He cited his complete and total endorsement from President Donald Trump and highlighted polling data showing him leading by more than 40 points in multiple public surveys. The congressman has raised $81 million for his campaign so far and indicated he would prefer to preserve those resources for the general election rather than spend them fighting rival Republicans in the primary. He stressed that all other candidates currently poll in single digits and contended that continued infighting among Republicans only benefits Democrats. "At this point, fighting amongst Republicans only helps the Democrats end the Florida Dream we all love and cherish," Donalds said. He pledged to communicate directly with voters through town halls, community meetings, business roundtables, and door-knocking efforts rather than through debate stage appearances.

However, two of Donalds' main competitors reject his call for unity and are demanding that he participate in debates. Jay Collins launched The Collins Callout website Friday, framing the challenge in confrontational terms. "The callout is on the table, the only question left is whether Byron answers the bell, or keeps running," the site stated. Former House Speaker Paul Renner went further, releasing a video on social media claiming that neither Donalds nor Collins is willing to debate him. "Floridians deserve to see the differences between the candidates. Stop ducking and let's get on stage," Renner said.

The candidates' fundraising totals through the end of March reveal significant gaps in their resources. Donalds has far outraised his opponents, while Renner had accumulated more than $6 million and Collins approximately $1.75 million. Updated fundraising reports covering activity through May will be due June 10, providing fresh indicators of financial momentum heading into the final stretch of the primary campaign. These figures underscore Donalds' substantial advantage in the field as the race enters its final phase.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds speaks out after receiving death threats in Florida gubernatorial race
cards.teaser: Gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds faced two separate death threats while campaigning for the Republican nomination in the August primary.
cards.body:
Gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds is speaking out about threats on his life as he runs for the Republican nomination in the August primary. The Naples Republican in his third term in Congress faced one threat on social media last month after re-sharing President Donald Trump's endorsement in the Governor's race. A second person called Donalds' district office making similar threats, saying he was going to blow up the entire office. "Somebody just flat out said they were going to kill me," Donalds told radio host Mark Levin on Friday.

Donalds cited the assassination of conservative Charlie Kirk last year as an example of what happens when political opponents are demonized rather than treated as human beings. He considers himself a free speech absolutist but stressed the importance of being mindful of rhetoric to avoid creating an environment where someone takes it as their responsibility to harm another person. "That's just reprehensible to me," he said. Donalds noted that recent experience shows examples of viewpoints being used to justify political violence and that people have strong opinions but ultimately just want to go home and see their families. He said the incident strengthened his resolve to work hard to become the state's next governor and keep Florida the preeminent conservative and common sense state in America. Donalds is undeterred by the threats and expressing confidence in his position in the race to succeed Ron DeSantis.

cards.headline: Tampa City Council Chair seeks delay in Rays stadium CRA vote amid ongoing negotiations
cards.teaser: Tampa City Council Chair Alan Clendenin submitted a memo requesting the Tampa Bay Rays stadium item be deferred until at least July rather than being taken up by the Tampa CRA next week.
cards.body:
Tampa City Council Chair Alan Clendenin is pushing to delay a pending Community Redevelopment Agency discussion tied to the Tampa Bay Rays stadium proposal, saying the issue is not ready for a vote as negotiations continue. Clendenin submitted a memo last week asking that the Rays item be deferred until at least July, and possibly longer, rather than being taken up by the Tampa CRA the following week as originally planned. He added that recent uncertainty over property tax reform has added another factor for negotiators to consider. The Rays stadium MOU approved by Tampa and Hillsborough County last month includes $80 million from the city of Tampa and another $100 million tied to the Tampa CRA, in addition to other public dollars.

Clendenin sharply disputed Hillsborough County Commissioner Joshua Wostal's characterization of where negotiations stand, clarifying that behind-the-scenes talks are still ongoing. He said the financing structure remains under active negotiation and that the scheduled discussion would be premature. Clendenin noted that earlier votes by the City Council and County Commission represented support for the general direction of the non-binding MOU, but not final approval of the CRA terms. Several options remain on the table for the CRA-related portion of the deal, including not using the CRA, creating a different type of district or using another special district structure. For the CRA portion, nothing has been agreed to by any party, Clendenin said.

cards.headline: Democrat Benjamin Sandlin launches second run for Jacksonville House District 12
cards.teaser: Benjamin Sandlin filed for the Jacksonville House race Friday, just three days before qualifying begins Monday. The 22-year-old lost the Republican-leaning seat by 14 points in 2024.
cards.body:
Democrat Benjamin Sandlin is launching a second run in Jacksonville's HD 12, where he lost by 14 points to House Speaker Pro Tempore Wyman Duggan two years ago. The Republican-leaning seat is open because Duggan is term-limited. The 22-year-old candidate filed for the House race Friday, just three days before the beginning of qualifying on Monday, June 8. Sandlin said the Florida Democratic Party and he had been talking and that they agreed this seat was just too close in 24 to leave uncontested. He told Florida Politics on Saturday morning that running would be a huge missed opportunity to have an extra voice for labor rights, public schools and housing justice in the Legislature. As the sole Democrat in HD 12, it is likely Sandlin will advance to the November ballot upon qualifying.

Former Jacksonville City Council President Terrance Freeman is running in HD 12 to succeed Duggan. Freeman is well-positioned for his Primary, having raised more than $167,000 to his campaign account and an additional $506,000 to an affiliated political committee, For the Future We Want, through the end of May. He had roughly $390,000 on hand at the end of last month. Freeman was appointed to the Jacksonville City Council in 2018 by former Gov. Rick Scott to fill a vacancy and was then elected to an at-large, countywide seat twice in 2019 and 2023, and served a year as Council President. He has announced he will resign from the Council once a replacement is elected, which could be as soon as August. Republican Deborah Wesley, a Jacksonville Sheriff's Office Commander, is the only filed candidate for the Special Election for the seat and has raised more than $80,000 as of the end of May.

cards.headline: Former Lake County Property Appraiser Carey Baker enters race for Congress in CD 11
cards.teaser: Carey Baker is running to succeed retiring U.S. Rep. Daniel Webster in CD 11. The 63-year-old is poised for a GOP Primary with Lake County Commissioner Anthony Sabatini.
cards.body:
Former Lake County Property Appraiser Carey Baker is running to succeed retiring U.S. Rep. Daniel Webster in Florida's 11th Congressional District. The 63-year-old represented much of the Central Florida district in Florida's Legislature, serving in both the House and Senate before being elected countywide as a constitutional official. Baker, a lifelong resident of Eustis, most recently served multiple terms as Property Appraiser. He lost re-election in 2024 after filing as a write-in candidate, with David Jordan defeating him by a 3-to-1 margin in the General Election. Despite the loss, Baker demonstrated fundraising prowess, raising $233,000 for the campaign. After the latest round of Congressional redistricting, Florida's 11th Congressional District includes all of Sumter County, some of west Orange County and most of Lake County.

Baker is poised for a GOP Primary with Lake County Commissioner Anthony Sabatini, who has already run for the seat. CD 11 is likely to be Republican in November, with more than 57% of voters there backing President Donald Trump in the 2024 Presidential Election. On Saturday, repeat Democratic candidate Barbie Harden Hall suspended her campaign due to health issues. Three other Democratic candidates, Royal Webster, Shawn Bettis, and Dan Williams, remain in the race for the nomination, though Hall was the leading fundraiser and seemed best-positioned to become the party's choice for a second time.

cards.headline: Raúl Castro makes first appearance since US indictment at 95th birthday celebration
cards.teaser: Cuba's former president appeared in public for the first time since being indicted by the United States for his alleged role in the 1996 downing of two civilian aircraft flown by Miami-based exiles.
cards.body:
Raúl Castro, Cuba's low-profile former president and revolutionary guerilla, appeared in public for the first time since being indicted by the United States for his alleged role in the 1996 downing of two civilian aircraft, official video released Saturday showed. Castro's celebration of his 95th birthday with top officials and military leaders at the Ministry of Interior in Havana on late Friday offered Cuba's socialist government an opportunity to close ranks and project defiance as the Trump administration escalates its pressure campaign on the fuel-starved island. State TV broadcast footage of Castro, clad in his olive-green military uniform, entering a packed theater to a standing ovation, followed by his grandson and bodyguard, Raúl Guillermo Rodríguez, and Cuban President Miguel Díaz-Canel.

Díaz-Canel delivered an effusive tribute to the heroism and dignity displayed by Castro and his late brother, Fidel Castro, praising Raúl Castro for his service as defense minister of Cuba for nearly 50 years. The celebration marked a rare public appearance for the influential Cuban army general, who formally retired from politics in April 2021 but is believed to wield considerable political power. The Justice Department's indictment unsealed last month accuses Castro of ordering the 1996 shootdown of civilian planes flown by Miami-based exiles. The Trump administration demands that Cuba's socialist government release political prisoners, implement major economic reforms and change its way of governance to avoid becoming a national security threat.

cards.headline: Senator Rick Scott remembers father who parachuted behind enemy lines on D-Day
cards.teaser: Senator Rick Scott honored his adopted father Orba Scott, who parachuted behind enemy lines during the 1944 D-Day operation in Normandy.
cards.body:
Senator Rick Scott is keeping the memory of World War II alive. On Saturday, the Naples Republican and Navy veteran is remembering what many members of the military had to do on D-Day, the famous 1944 World War II military operation wherein more than 160,000 Allied troops stormed the beaches of Normandy and made first headway in the liberation of German-occupied France. Orba Scott, who raised the Senator, was among those engaged in the operation. As the Senator recounts, his adopted dad parachuted behind enemy lines and selflessly fought for the well-being and freedom of Americans and families across the world.

My father was blessed enough to return home from battle, but many brave individuals made the last full measure of devotion in defense of freedom and didn't return home, Sen. Scott said. The Senator vows to continue fighting for those who have fought for America. As a Navy veteran and the son of an Army veteran, Scott said he is fighting every day to improve the military, take care of the nation's veterans, and protect their legacy so the next generation knows and appreciates the sacrifices made for their freedoms.

hero.headline: 35 foster youth graduate at ChildNet celebration
hero.teaser: Thirty-five foster youth and young adults walked across the stage at ChildNet's annual graduation celebration at Palm Beach State College.
hero.body:
ChildNet marked a significant milestone by hosting its annual graduation celebration at Palm Beach State College, where 35 students participated in the ceremony. The nonprofit organization serves foster youth and young adults across Broward and Palm Beach counties, providing support through education programs, adoption services and independent living resources designed to help young people transition to adulthood.

Among the graduates were Sabrina Diaz and Brian Saintfort, two students who have overcome substantial challenges with ChildNet's assistance. Both lost a parent during their time in the foster care system and relied on the organization to provide the resources they needed to move forward with their lives. Diaz is currently enrolled in pre-med classes at Palm Beach State College with aspirations of becoming a doctor. Saintfort has chosen a different path, planning to pursue a vocational program to become a plumber. Their diverse goals reflect the range of opportunities available to graduates supported by the organization.

During the celebration, both graduates shared messages of encouragement for other young people in similar circumstances. Diaz emphasized the importance of maintaining hope and perseverance through difficult times. "Belief that you're going to be big one day and just put effort into it, never give up on school and never give up on dreams. If you like push past with the pain and just keep trying hard," she said. Saintfort similarly stressed the power of self-belief in achieving success. "Believe that you'll make it, then you're gonna make it and stuff," he said.

ChildNet CEO Larry N. Rein used the occasion to acknowledge the collective effort that made the evening possible. He highlighted the contributions of case workers from both ChildNet and the Department of Children and Family Services, while particularly praising the graduates themselves for their hard work and determination. "This evening is the fruition of great work by everyone in the community, including case workers at ChildNet, DCF and especially the kids who have worked so hard. We are to celebrate them!" Rein said. The graduation celebration demonstrated how comprehensive support systems, combined with the resilience of young people in foster care, can help overcome obstacles and create pathways to successful futures.

cards.headline: Brief law enforcement pursuit slows northbound I-95 traffic near Hobe Sound
cards.teaser: A short law enforcement pursuit caused traffic delays on northbound Interstate 95 near Hobe Sound on Friday.
cards.body:
Law enforcement engaged in a brief pursuit that slowed northbound traffic on Interstate 95 near Hobe Sound. The incident occurred Friday evening and affected motorists traveling north through the area.

The pursuit impacted traffic flow on the northbound lanes of I-95 in the Hobe Sound area. Drivers experienced slowdowns as the law enforcement activity unfolded on the interstate.

The chase was brief and traffic conditions were affected temporarily as the situation developed near Hobe Sound. The pursuit took place on one of the main traffic corridors through Martin County.

cards.headline: Stuart unveils massive mural to promote ecosystem awareness
cards.teaser: The city of Stuart has unveiled a large mural designed to promote awareness of the local ecosystem.
cards.body:
Stuart revealed a massive mural intended to increase public awareness about the ecosystem. The mural was unveiled on Saturday in the city.

The artwork promotes environmental consciousness and draws attention to ecosystem issues relevant to the Stuart area. City officials presented the mural to the public this weekend.

The large-scale mural represents an effort to educate residents and visitors about the importance of the local ecosystem. The unveiling took place in Stuart on Saturday.

cards.headline: Martin County revamps emergency dispatch center
cards.teaser: Martin County has upgraded its emergency dispatch center with new improvements to the facility.
cards.body:
The county overhauled the dispatch center that handles emergency calls for Martin County residents. The upgrades represent a modernization of the emergency response infrastructure.

The revamped dispatch center will serve the county's emergency services coordination. Martin County announced the completion of the facility improvements on Saturday morning.

cards.headline: Vote open for best restaurant in Port Salerno area
cards.teaser: Residents can vote for the best restaurant in the Port Salerno area of Stuart.
cards.body:
A vote is underway to determine the best restaurant in the Port Salerno area. The voting opportunity was announced on Saturday for restaurants in the Stuart community.

Residents can participate in selecting the top dining establishment in Port Salerno. The vote focuses on restaurants located in the Port Salerno section of Stuart.

The voting process allows community members to weigh in on their favorite local restaurants. The poll covers dining options available in the Port Salerno area.

cards.headline: Martin County Fire Rescue extinguishes nearly 40-acre brush fire in Indiantown
cards.teaser: Martin County Fire Rescue extinguished a brush fire that burned nearly 40 acres in Indiantown.
cards.body:
Martin County Fire Rescue extinguished a brush fire that burned nearly 40 acres in Indiantown. The fire was reported on Friday and crews worked to contain the blaze.

Firefighters battled the flames in the Indiantown area of Martin County. The fire scorched close to 40 acres before being brought under control.

Martin County Fire Rescue responded to the incident and worked to prevent the fire from spreading further. Crews successfully extinguished the fire after it had consumed the acreage.

The brush fire marked a significant response for Martin County Fire Rescue in the Indiantown community. The department brought the fire under control and prevented additional damage to the area.

cards.headline: Brian Warren of Stuart remembered
cards.teaser: Brian Warren, a Stuart resident, is being remembered by family and friends.
cards.body:
Brian Warren of Stuart passed away in 2026. All County Funeral Home & Crematory Treasure Coast Chapel in Stuart is handling arrangements.

Warren was a resident of Stuart. The funeral home serving the family is located on the Treasure Coast.

Family and friends are remembering Warren following his death. Services are being coordinated through the Stuart funeral home.

hero.headline: Fertilizer Ban Now in Effect in Indian River County
hero.teaser: A fertilizer ban is now active in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties.
hero.body:
Indian River County is under a fertilizer ban along with Martin and St. Lucie counties. The restriction applies to residential and commercial fertilizer application during the designated period.

The ban covers all three Treasure Coast counties as part of seasonal environmental protections. The restriction is designed to reduce nutrient runoff into local waterways during the rainy season.

cards.headline: Texas Rangers Youth Academy Team to Play in Vero Beach June 17
cards.teaser: The Texas Rangers Youth Academy will field a team in the 2026 Breakthrough Series Invitational starting June 17 in Vero Beach.
cards.body:
The Texas Rangers Youth Academy 2026 Breakthrough Series Invitational team is set to debut in Vero Beach on June 17. The team will compete in the tournament hosted in the city.

The Breakthrough Series Invitational will bring the Texas Rangers youth program to Vero Beach for the competition. The event is scheduled to begin next week at facilities in Vero Beach.

cards.headline: Vero Beach Police Chief Defends Search for Slaying Suspect Jesse Ellis
cards.teaser: The Vero Beach Police Chief said officers did all they could to find slaying suspect Jesse Ellis, according to a statement released Friday.
cards.body:
The Vero Beach Police Chief said officers did all they could to find slaying suspect Jesse Ellis, according to a statement released Friday. The comments come as the department faces questions about the search for Ellis in connection with a homicide investigation.

The chief's statement addressed the efforts made by the Vero Beach Police Department to locate Ellis. Law enforcement officials have been working to apprehend the suspect in the slaying case.

The case remains an active investigation by Vero Beach police. Ellis is wanted in connection with the homicide that occurred in the city.

The police chief's defense of the department's search efforts comes as the investigation continues. Vero Beach police are still seeking information on Ellis's whereabouts.

cards.headline: Dolphin Entanglements in Indian River Lagoon Rising, Scientists Say
cards.teaser: Wildlife scientists report a skyrocketing number of dolphins entangled in fishing line in the Indian River Lagoon.
cards.body:
Wildlife scientists expressed concern about the increasing number of dolphin and fishing line entanglement cases in the Indian River Lagoon. The incidents involve dolphins becoming trapped in fishing gear and other marine debris.

The rise in entanglement cases has alarmed researchers monitoring the lagoon's marine mammal population. Scientists tracking the issue say the number of dolphins affected by fishing line has increased significantly in recent months.

cards.headline: Indian River County Recycling Club Offers 2026 Scholarships
cards.teaser: The Recycling Club of Indian River County announced college scholarship opportunities for 2026.
cards.body:
The Recycling Club of Indian River County announced the availability of college scholarship opportunities for 2026. The organization is accepting applications from eligible students in the county.

The scholarship program is designed to support students pursuing higher education. The Recycling Club of Indian River County administers the awards to local applicants meeting the program requirements.

cards.body:
